name: rustls
workload: TLS 1.2/1.3 full handshake and resumed handshake rate, bulk AES128-GCM send/receive throughput, and per-session memory footprint; rustls 0.22.0 (aws-lc crypto provider) vs OpenSSL 3.2.0, from the aochagavia/rustls-bench-results 2023 ISRG-funded benchmark.
claimed_speedup: TLS1.2 full handshake (client): 4,992 vs 2,581 handshakes/sec (1.93x); resumed handshakes 80-330% more per second; AES128-GCM send 6,712 vs 6,504 MB/s (1.03x) but receive 6,018 vs 7,234 MB/s (0.83x, slower); ~13KiB vs ~69KiB memory per session, 131.8MB vs 688.4MB for 10,000 concurrent sessions (-81%); ChaCha20-Poly1305 throughput ~45% slower than OpenSSL
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.2.0 and Clang 14.0.6 (specific optimization flags not itemized on the summary page)
stars_or_usage: 7.6k stars; used in curl, AWS, Cloudflare and other production TLS stacks
tradeoffs: Mixed results depending on cipher/direction: faster handshakes, resumption, and far lower memory use, but slower AES128-GCM receive throughput and notably slower ChaCha20-Poly1305 throughput than OpenSSL on this hardware; numbers are tied to the aws-lc crypto backend chosen for rustls, not rustls's own crypto code.
caveats: Numbers were read from the bencher.dev case-study summary of the aochagavia/rustls-bench-results dashboard (2023 run) plus a 2019 jbp.io post; exact compiler flags are not fully itemized. rustls is itself one of the three named incumbent baselines for this category (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, rustls), so this entry documents rustls's own standing vs OpenSSL rather than a third-party project beating rustls.
found_via: Hacker News: query 'rustls faster than OpenSSL' -> https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39766805 ("How Rustls fights to stay faster than OpenSSL")

name: AWS-LC
workload: Full TLS handshake connections/sec (server-only) and TLS session-resumption connections/sec under HAProxy, on a 64-core AWS Graviton4 instance, across OpenSSL 1.1.1/3.0.x/3.1-3.4-dev, AWS-LC, and WolfSSL.
claimed_speedup: Full handshake: AWS-LC (optimized, RSA opts + CMAKE_C_STANDARD=11) 63,000+ conn/sec vs OpenSSL 1.1.1 ~48,000 and OpenSSL 3.0.2 ~21,000 (up to ~3x vs OpenSSL 3.0.2). TLS resumption (with HAProxy low-overhead locks): AWS-LC (C11 build) 183,000 conn/sec vs OpenSSL 1.1.1 124,000, OpenSSL 3.0.14 8,000 (AWS-LC ~23x), and OpenSSL 3.0.2 1,500-1,600 (AWS-LC ~114-122x, collapsing above 16 threads due to lock contention).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-11.4; AWS-LC rebuilt with CMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 (vs default C99) to enable atomics instead of pthread locks; HAProxy built with USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION=1 for low-overhead locks
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores, Ubuntu 22.04
license: Apache-2.0 (ISC and OpenSSL license portions for imported code)
stars_or_usage: used in production AWS services (s2n-tls, AWS SDKs); GitHub page showed ~835 stars at fetch time
tradeoffs: Extreme resumption speedup is largely an OpenSSL-3.x-specific lock-contention pathology, not purely an AWS-LC design win over OpenSSL 1.1.1 (gap there is much smaller, ~1.3x-1.5x); requires a non-default C11 build flag to hit peak numbers.
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark by HAProxy Technologies (Willy Tarreau, William Lallemand), published 2025-05-06, using their own open-source h1load load generator (https://github.com/wtarreau/h1load); this is a Tier-A benchmark for AWS-LC, which is already on the known-projects list, so is_evidence_for_known is set true per the harness exception rule.
found_via: Hacker News comment: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46628936 (search 'TLS faster OpenSSL', tags=comment) linking to haproxy.com/blog/state-of-ssl-stacks

name: wolfSSL
workload: Same HAProxy full-handshake and TLS-resumption connections/sec benchmark on a 64-core AWS Graviton4 instance, comparing WolfSSL 5.7.0 against OpenSSL 1.1.1/3.0.x/3.1-3.4-dev and AWS-LC.
claimed_speedup: Full handshake: WolfSSL 5.7.0 ~48,000 conn/sec, on par with OpenSSL 1.1.1 (~48,000) and ~2.3x OpenSSL 3.0.2 (~21,000). TLS resumption: WolfSSL 150,000 conn/sec vs OpenSSL 1.1.1 124,000 (1.2x), OpenSSL 3.0.14 8,000 (~19x), and OpenSSL 3.0.2 1,500-1,600 (~94-100x, the latter collapsing under thread contention).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-11.4; HAProxy built with USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION=1 for low-overhead locks
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores, Ubuntu 22.04
stars_or_usage: 2.9k stars; widely used in embedded/IoT TLS deployments
tradeoffs: GPL licensing (vs OpenSSL's Apache-2.0) requires a commercial license for closed-source distribution; large resumption speedup over OpenSSL 3.x is amplified by OpenSSL's own lock-contention regression rather than solely WolfSSL's design.
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark by HAProxy Technologies, published 2025-05-06, using the open-source h1load tool; Tier-A benchmark for wolfSSL, which is already on the known-projects list, so is_evidence_for_known is set true per the harness exception rule.
found_via: Hacker News comment: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46628936 (search 'TLS faster OpenSSL', tags=comment) linking to haproxy.com/blog/state-of-ssl-stacks

name: ring
workload: TLS-handshake crypto-operation micro-benchmark (hyperfine) across 3 key agreements x 5 signature algorithms x 3 cipher suites, run inside the WTX project comparing aws-lc-rs, Graviola, ring, and OpenSSL as pluggable crypto backends.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only: author states 'OpenSSL is the slower library' across ECDSA/Ed25519/RSA-PSS scenarios and that ring is competitive with/faster than the others in most cases; exact execution-time numbers are rendered only as SVG bar charts (not machine-readable text) and could not be extracted as a numeric ratio without risking an invented figure.
compiler_and_flags: Unstated/uncertain; the author explicitly notes 'it is unknown if the root cause is a missing compile flag' for OpenSSL's worse showing
license: Custom permissive composite (Apache-2.0 and ISC, with portions under OpenSSL/BoringSSL-derived licenses; see LICENSE, LICENSE-BoringSSL, LICENSE-other-bits)
stars_or_usage: 4.1k stars; used transitively via rustls/quinn/tokio ecosystem
tradeoffs: Deliberately minimal, low-level unsafe-adjacent API by design (no general-purpose TLS API of its own); non-standard composite license complicates SPDX classification/compliance tooling.
caveats: Single independent blogger's benchmark (author of the unrelated WTX project) using hyperfine over 36 build combinations; numeric results are only in SVG bar charts, not stated as text, so no precise ratio could be reported; compiler flags unconfirmed, capping the tier at C rather than B.
found_via: Hacker News: query 'TLS handshake performance' -> https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48890397 ("TLS Handshakes: Measuring the Performance of 4 Cryptography Libraries")

name: aws-lc-rs
workload: Same WTX-project TLS-handshake crypto-operation micro-benchmark (hyperfine) as the ring entry above; aws-lc-rs backend measured against OpenSSL, ring, and Graviola for ECDSA/Ed25519/RSA-PSS handshake operations.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only: outperforms OpenSSL generally ('OpenSSL is the slower library') but the author notes aws-lc-rs is 'not as fast as ring or Graviola when dealing with RSA-PSS'; no numeric ratio is given as text (values only in SVG charts).
stars_or_usage: 655 stars (Rust-bindings crate); underlying aws-lc C library used in production AWS TLS stacks
tradeoffs: Wraps the C aws-lc library via FFI; RSA-PSS handshake path is comparatively slower than ring/Graviola per this benchmark; larger binary footprint than pure-Rust alternatives.
caveats: Same single-blog benchmark limitations as the ring entry: SVG-only numeric charts, compiler flags unconfirmed, capped at Tier C. This is a distinct repo (github.com/aws/aws-lc-rs, Rust bindings) from the already-catalogued C library github.com/aws/aws-lc, so it is not excluded by the known-projects list.
found_via: Hacker News: query 'TLS handshake performance' -> https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48890397 ("TLS Handshakes: Measuring the Performance of 4 Cryptography Libraries")
